stops.name: Ganja, the death of the poet
stops.campa: Having built the five treasures without leaving his city, Nizami dies in Ganja in his sixty-eighth year, his son Muhammad grown, his quintet complete and already copied outward across the Persian world. The Panj Ganj, the Five Treasures, will be illuminated for six centuries by the greatest painters of Persia, Herat, and India, the seven domes and the desert and the road through Behistun painted and repainted. The poet who scarcely traveled has sent five worlds out to conquer the earth in his place.
stops.quote: In the treasury of Ganja I laid five treasures; go, my words, and I shall stay.
stops.quote_source: Nizami, closing sense of the Khamsa (Panj Ganj, 'Five Treasures'; biographical tradition)

stops.name: The Nizami Mausoleum, the tomb outside Ganja
stops.campa: They raise a tomb of white limestone over his grave outside Ganja, and there it stands and is rebuilt across the centuries: first noted in the chronicles in 1606, raised anew in the twentieth century as a tall cylinder of dark stone in a garden, a metal statue of his heroes beside it. Pilgrims still come. The man who made the horizon a wife's name, who moved a mountain in verse for love, who sent a king into the dark after a water he would not drink, lies here in the city he never left, and the five worlds keep travelling without him.
